summary: Describes how to use the ATM call-setup procedures from UNI Signalling 4.0 efficiently to support IP over ATM networks. It is on the standards track and builds on earlier IP over ATM work.

plainLanguage.summary: How to ask an old-style phone-like network to set up a connection so internet traffic can ride over it.

what is atm signalling for ip
what is ubr for ip over atm
what is frame discard in atm
subtitle: How IP systems should fill in ATM UNI 4.0 call setup messages to get sensible best-effort connections.

tldr.problem: UNI Signalling 4.0 added many new options, such as Available Bit Rate and traffic parameter negotiation, and IP over ATM implementations needed guidance on which ones to use and how.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the information elements a SETUP message MUST carry for IP, gives the values to use for AAL 5 and LLC/SNAP, and recommends UBR with negotiation, plus frame discard, as the default for best-effort IP.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 1755 for UNI 4.0 and applies only to plain best-effort IP, not to IP with Integrated Services.

today: RFC 2331 is a Proposed Standard published in April 1998, and its metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a follow-on to RFC 1755.

sections.title: Scope and What Is New in SIG 4.0
sections.content:
RFC 2331 explains how to use the call control procedures of UNI Signalling 4.0 (SIG 4.0) to support IP over ATM as described in RFC 2225 and RFC 2332. It follows RFC 1755, which was based on UNI 3.1, and assumes the reader knows that RFC.

Of the new SIG 4.0 features, the memo covers three: ABR signalling for point-to-point calls, traffic parameter negotiation and frame discard. Leaf Initiated Join, Anycast and Switched VP service are not discussed because models for using them with IP over ATM have not been defined.

The memo applies only to IP as the plain best-effort connectionless service. IP with Integrated Services is left to other specifications from the ISSLL working group.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone network got new buttons. This memo says which of the new buttons are useful for ordinary internet traffic, and ignores the fancy ones nobody knows how to use yet.

sections.title: Teardown and SETUP Contents
sections.content:
For VC teardown, a system with a Public ATM UNI that is the called party of a VCC MUST NOT use an inactivity timer on that VCC by default, though it MAY if configured to. This helps when layer 3 reservations such as RSVP map onto VCs, because the sender of a reserved flow should tear the VC down once the receiver stops refreshing the reservation.

A SETUP message for an IP or multiprotocol call MUST contain the AAL Parameters, ATM Traffic Descriptor, Broadband Bearer Capability, Broadband Low Layer Information, QoS Parameter, Called Party Number and Calling Party Number information elements. Several others, including the new Minimum Acceptable and Alternative ATM Traffic Descriptors and the ABR parameter elements, MAY appear. AAL Parameters and Broadband Low Layer Information are optional in SIG 4.0 itself, but MUST be included for IP over ATM.
sections.plainLanguage: Every call request has to carry a set of filled-in boxes, such as who is calling, who is being called, and what kind of line is wanted. The memo lists the boxes that cannot be left empty for internet calls.

sections.title: Key Information Elements
sections.content:
The AAL Parameters element selects AAL 5 with a null SSCS, and carries maximum SDU sizes in each direction equal to the desired IP MTU. The example shows 65,535, but the memo notes that in practice most sites have used 9180 IP MTUs. The Broadband Low Layer Information element selects LLC/SNAP encapsulation with layer_2_id 2 and user_information_layer 12. Both are meaningful only to the endpoints, and the network does not process them.

Traffic is described by the ATM Traffic Descriptor, Broadband Bearer Capability (which gained an ATM Transfer Capability field in SIG 4.0) and QoS Parameter elements. The QoS Parameter element may be omitted only if the Extended QoS Parameters element is present. The memo makes no explicit recommendation on QoS elements.

Addresses go in the Called and Calling Party Number elements, and an endsystem learns its own ATM address using ILMI 4.0.
sections.plainLanguage: One box says how big a package can be, another says how the package is wrapped, and others say who is calling whom.

sections.title: Traffic Choices and Negotiation
sections.content:
A site may be configured for any ATM service category: CBR, loss-permitting CBR, ABR, UBR, real-time VBR and non-real-time VBR. Because a non-IIS IP service has no idea of the needs of higher layers, the memo says UBR, the best-effort category, is the most natural, and if a site allows it, users SHOULD signal for UBR.

UBR comes in two modes. UBR.1 disables tagging and UBR.2 enables it. If the terminal shapes its traffic or the network does not enforce the peak cell rate, the user SHOULD ask for no tagging (UBR.1). If the network enforces the peak cell rate and the source does not shape, the user SHOULD ask for tagging (UBR.2).

SIG 4.0 lets some traffic parameters be negotiated during setup, but not renegotiated once the call is active. A SETUP or CONNECT may include only one of the Minimum Acceptable ATM Traffic Descriptor (for PCR) or the Alternative ATM Traffic Descriptor. IP over ATM entities SHOULD ask for a PCR equal to the link rate and a minimum PCR of zero.
sections.plainLanguage: For everyday internet traffic, the plain best-effort line is the right pick. You ask for the fastest speed the road allows, and you tell the network it is fine if you only get a slower one.

sections.title: ABR and Frame Discard
sections.content:
Two information elements support Available Bit Rate signalling: ABR Setup Parameters and ABR Additional Parameters. The memo describes their subfields but gives no advice on when to use ABR for IP VCCs or what values to pick.

Appendix B suggests that routers joined by ATM may want a non-zero bandwidth commitment for their aggregate traffic. For ABR the end system should specify the Peak Cell Rate, the Minimum Cell Rate and the Cumulative RM Fixed Round-Trip Time, and QoS Class 0 MUST be requested. For non-real-time VBR, the suggestion is VBR.3 with PCR, SCR and MBS specified and both tagging and frame discard requested.

Frame discard is based on Partial and Early Packet Discard. Frame discard signalling MUST be supported by all IP over ATM entities, and the memo RECOMMENDS signalling it for all IP SVCs, because it has been shown to raise throughput under congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: If a package gets damaged, the rest of that package is useless anyway. So the network is told to throw away whole packages, not random bits, which keeps things moving.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The ATM Forum security group had not yet produced a specification, so the memo says it is premature to define how IP over ATM signalling would use ATM security. Without it, the originator of signalling messages such as connection setup or teardown requests cannot be authenticated. The memo notes that IP Security (RFC 1825) can be applied to IP datagrams over ATM VCs to make up for the missing security at the ATM layer.
sections.plainLanguage: At the time, the phone network had no way to check who was really asking for a call. So the memo says to lock the messages themselves instead.
